It was worth the extra time to grease everything when I assembled it. I didn't see the need for a water bottle so I cut off the top third and use it to hold my tv remote. The Dvds are terrible! It's become a much-used club in my bag and I'd say it's cut several strokes off my game. Quality of the club exceeded my expectations. Here in the northeast, this last season offered two basic turf conditions: dry as concrete or soggy, muddy slop. Neither condition makes it easy to use a wedge for those close shots under 75 yards. text_fidelity_a:
Lockdown Gun Concealment Magnet , Black The Lockdown Gun Magnet is almost... almost what I needed.

It has the two thicker discs, connected by ferrous metal, with a soft rubber coating. The magnetism is on the logo'd side; it won't even hold itself up against a fridge on the other side. So make sure you mount it correct-side-out.

It seems nicely made and equipped. The rubber is non-scuffing and won't hurt the guns. The screw-holes are counter-sunk. It comes with drywall anchors and three lengths of black screws. (The packaging claims two sets of screws.) Both sides of it are rubber-coated, so no rattles or vibrations. The first impressions are great.

It is decently strong; it can lift a 5-pound weight disk. But that's a pretty perfect case; flat metal, smooth, full contact, being lifted straight up. And it isn't a strong grip on the 5-pound disk; you can shake it loose pretty easily.

And that's the problem. A typical handgun (e.g. Star Firestar - 2#, Browning Hi-Power 2.3#, Colt 1911 2.5#) weighs about half that weight disk... but it doesn't have all the metal on the surface and doesn't have a smooth flat contact patch. So the Lockdown doesn't hold a typical handgun tightly enough for the odd placement and motion in a vehicle. In fairness, the Kahr PM9 is about 1.3 # loaded, the Beretta Nano 9mm about 1.1# loaded and the Colt Mustang Pocketlite .380 and Beretta Pico .380 barely 3/4-pound, but they also have less ferrous metal in them for the magnets to grip.
text_fidelity_b: Lockdown Gun Concealment Magnet , Black

Sunny Health & Fitness Indoor Cycling Exercise Bike with Heavy-Duty 49 LB Chrome Flywheel, Stationary Bike with Customizable Comfort with 275 LBS. Max Weight I struggled between the high-end spin bikes and this one. "You get what you pay for" kept going through my head. I eventually settled on the lower cost option since it was my first; I figured if I could get 2-3 years out of it I could upgrade later. The box arrived in pristine condition, which was a pleasant surprise. It arrived less that 48 hours from the time I ordered it. It took about 30 minutes to put together by myself, nothing was too difficult. I've been using it every day. It is "whisper-quiet" as I've seen described. I prefer more resistance and with the 46lb flywheel its a real workout. I had an elliptical for my pre-workout cardio for about 5 years (it finally completely broke apart) and the spin bike beats it hands down. I added a inexpensive Velo 7 speedometer to see that my speed is consistent (important for road biking) and that works great too. Although this spin bike doesn't have micro-adjustments for the handlebar and seat I was lucky to find a setting on each that fits my body type.

My only negative comment, and this is a real stretch to find something negative to say...is regarding the resistance pad/brake. I keep a can of silicon spray next to my spin bike and every 4-5 days give the pad a quick shot because it starts getting a little noisy. If/when I eventually do upgrade I might look at a spin bike with magnetic resistance but to get the belt drive with magnetic resistance you can increase the cost 3x.

I haven't seen any follow up comments to reviews for purchases 2-3 years ago and I'm hopeful that, with care, this spin bike will last many years with the occasional replacement belt and/or brake pad and regular maintenance.

To sum up my thoughts on this spin bike...it's inexpensive but its not cheap...it's well made and works great!
text_fidelity_b: Sunny Health & Fitness Indoor Cycling Exercise Bike with Heavy-Duty 49 LB Chrome Flywheel, Stationary Bike with Customizable Comfort with 275 LBS. Max Weight

text_fidelity_a:
Napier Backroadz SUV Tent | Universal Fits All CUV’s, SUV’s, and Minivans​ | Sleeps 5 Adults | Grey & Green | 10'x10' (19100) I got this (obviously) because I wanted to do some car camping (also, obviously). All-in-all it's a very good design and I think it will work out well for me. But it does have some issues - including a misleading description - so I'll tell you about those too.

First, by myself, it was fairly easy to set up. It's a learning experience, so make sure you set it up in your yard before you're in some dispersed campsite in BF Outer Badlands. Running the poles was straightforward, but I found that Blue Tape is your friend when attaching the main poles to the corner fittings. A second person might make the tape unnecessary, but it would still make it easier. Getting the main structure set - for the first time - took about 20 minutes, the whole set up took about an hour but I was being slow and deliberate. The inside is great and the HUGE windows provide ample ventilation. If anything the tent is too tall (which makes it tough to put the rainfly on solo) but there's plenty of room to stand everywhere in the tent. The connection with the car is good but, as others have noted, you will get some gaps (especially if you have a roof rack) that will allow bugs to get in.

Now, the big downside. The rainfly and construction is described as offering the "ultimate weather protection". Not even close. While the fly's seams are sealed, the fabric itself relies on the weave to let more water run off than soak through. The night after my initial setup there was a light dew and the rainfly was as wet on the inside as it was on the outside. The only part of the tent that seems truly waterproof is the floor. I'm planning on waterproofing the fly, the whole front door panel of the tent, any part of the tent exposed under the fly, and seal all the seams. Pay particular attention to the ground seam as it's completely exposed.

Quality control was spotty. There were some poorly stitched seams (picture) that shouldn't have made it past QC. Also, the slide locks for the fly guy ropes were incorrectly tied so I had to take them apart and retie them (picture) to keep them from slipping. Not a big deal but indicative that somebody is not paying attention. (Note: There are a couple of different ways to tie a slide lock, one of which only uses the end holes, so I don't know why they made a 3-hole lock.) The guy ropes themselves are invisible in the dark. They're flecked with white but are not reflective so another corner cut (and thing to fix...)

Bottom line is a good design with some issues that need to be fixed to make it a usable tent.

Update - I've upped it a star. I just came back from my first camping trip using the tent. It went very well. The tent is very easy to setup solo. The screen material was 100% (well, 99.99%) effective at keeping the bugs out (and it was *very* buggy) and the height of the tent makes for very comfortable living. My original comments stand as to construction, etc, but I had a problem with a weak piece of fabric which I reported to Napier. Their customer service department was amazing. They addressed the issue quickly and totally fixed things. That earned them the extra star.
text_fidelity_b: Napier Backroadz SUV Tent | Universal Fits All CUV’s, SUV’s, and Minivans​ | Sleeps 5 Adults | Grey & Green | 10'x10' (19100)

Keep in mind that I bought 2 of these cameras (yes I know, should have tried one first). Both work identically and both are totally useless for detecting game or people past 6 feet.

Both knives arrived oiled with the blades sharp. Each knife also has a drilled hole near the handle end for a lanyard if desired. Both of these are full tang knives and share a heavy duty sheath each having its own fitted sleeve/sheath. I had a hard time at first getting them in and out of the sheaths because of how tight they were, but the sheaths do start to loosen up as you remove the knifes and insert them back into the sheaths. The larger knife weighs 1 lb, 11 oz. The smaller knife weighs 7.3 oz. Both knives with the sheath have a combined weight of 2 lb, 10 oz. The sheath fits over a belt, and the belt strap is quite wide and looks to me like it should fit over most belt widths. At first I thought the sheath for the smaller knife could be detached by perhaps a snap or velcro, but the smaller knife sheath is strongly attached to the large sheath.

The only issue I found was along the outer edge of the smaller knife handle where the blade runs through the handle. The metal wasn't fully smooth and had what felt like microscopic burrs along the edge. I was able to smooth this with a super fine nail file, but had to be very careful in doing so such that I would not sand any of the wood on the handle. This only took me about a minute to do, but had to be done.

Aside from the little issue mentioned above which I was able to easily fix, I really love this set. Both knifes and sheaths are super strong, heavy duty and well-constructed. Great addition to any knife collection!

text_fidelity_a:
Coleman 100 Quart Xtreme 5 Wheeled Cooler Having owned one of these for a few years I feel more than qualified to review this.

- To the people who say it doesn't work, first "temper" the cooler. That means you bring it inside, put cold items in it and let it sit. I temper mine for several days before use.
- Second, use block ice. I use the square ice cream containers from Wally-World. They pack nicely, stack nicely and are easy for me to get in my freezer to make the blocks. Barring that, keep the ice you guy in bags. The greater the ice mass, the less quickly it melts. I also use water bottles filled close to the top. I'll freeze them, cap them after they're frozen and put them in the cooler. You've a double use: ice and cold water when it melts.
- Third, make sure the products you put in the cooler start out cold. Again, the colder they are, the longer they'll stay cold.
- Fourth, don't expect anything in direct sunlight or on hot ground to stay cold. If you need, park this on a couple blocks of wood to get it off the ground and get air flow under it. Hot ground will eventually cause the cooler to become hot. Insulation doesn't care whether it's keeping cold things cold or hot things hot. If you get it hot, it'll start making things inside hot.
- Lastly, if you have water and still have ice, that COLD water makes a good conductor of cool temperatures. If you drain the water you're not doing yourself a favor. You should have your foods in ziplock bags for best protection.

I've used this cooler on an extended trip to the Sequoias from Eastern Washington State. This rode in the back of my pick up with only a tarp for shade. The trip south took three days (owing to stops at family and friends). No additional ice required. Once at the campground, still no ice required.
We were at the campground a week. After that week we did drain off excess and add more ice. The return trip was through Lake Tahoe on to Nevada, staying at Carson City for three days, over to Oregon - staying in Ontario, OR and then back home. Yup, most of the ice had melted, but the larger pieces kept the water cold.

If you take care of your cooler, it should take care of you. The handle is nice and wide with an easy grip. The wheels move nicely and everything feels comfortable when pulling it along.
text_fidelity_b: Coleman 100 Quart Xtreme 5 Wheeled Cooler

All in all a very nice cooler keep everything dry in some reasonably heavy rain, and if it fell off the kayak.

For my use case a definite recommend and it will be part of my regular camp gear.

Nite Ize Spokelit Led Spoke Light - Best Bicycle Lights For Safety And Visibility - Steady Glow Or Flash, Blue Good Stuff: These fit fairly well on traditional spokes, and actually work on my flat/bladed spokes as well (Aksium road wheels). They produce a decent amount of light (I'm using 1 per wheel), and apparently get attention, and I've had the occasional stare or hoot from passing motorists, etc. These increased my side visibility a lot, and I use them on early-morning and night rides. I get a good amount of light from the blinking mode, so I suggest using that to conserve battery unless you're looking for a specific lighting effect, etc.

Bad stuff: The rubber/plastic body is kind of a press-fit on the spoke, so they'll wear down if you're moving them from wheel to wheel a lot--may not stay on the spokes quite as well after a few changes. Putting the light on the spoke also involves kind of a twist-and-slide motion, so you'll want to be kind of light-handed to avoid affecting the wheel's alignment/truing. As other reviewers noted, I got mine in with nearly-spent batteries (one had been on in transit, in the solid-on mode), though I bought the 25-pack-of-2016's, and it's been working OK so far. Also note: if you're riding a bike with narrow chainstays or a narrow front fork, you may want to check the positioning before riding with these--may not have a lot of room between light and frame because of the dome-shaped power button. I was able to make mine fit on a road frame (Orbea Onix), though I have be pretty scientific about where I position the light on the rear wheel.

Overall: for the price, I'd say these are a decent buy, and a relatively low-cost way to get some side visibility.

text_fidelity_a:
BLACKHAWK Men's Tac Convertible Long Sleeve Shirt I am a fan of the Blackhawk Warrior Lightweight Tactical Short Sleeve shirt, owning a few in each of the four offered colors. The Warrior shirt is made of a heavier material and is almost as flexible and handy as a tool box. It has two large front pockets that have Velcro fasteners. The right one has a smaller pocket inside it and also an opening at the top to slide a pen in. The left side pocket has a deep zippered pocket inside it and a ring hanging off the side for hanging your sunglasses. There is also a zippered pocket on the lower left side of the shirt that would be hidden if you tuck your shirt inside your pants/shorts.

On the left sleeve is a smaller pocket to carry anything up to about 5 inches long. Buttons are used to fasten the shirt. Although you can see through the material when you hold it up to the sun, it is heavy material (100% Polyester) and gets pretty warm in sunny Southwest Florida. The heavier material does keep the shirt looking crisp longer but the cut is pretty boxy as far as shape. There are three eyelets below the back of the collar for ventilation. An interesting feature is that the three vent holes are covered with mesh to keep biting insects out, a great feature for our climate. All-in-all the Blackhawk Warrior is a durable shirt that is double sewn and should last you a long time.

What about this new Tac Convertible Long Sleeve shirt? It appears to be mostly an improvement on the Warrior shirt. Although it is also made of 100% Polyester, it is significantly lighter and easier to see through if you hold it up to the sun. The fabric is designed to dry quickly and offers UPF 50 protection. The material is soft and the Teflon Shield+ fabric protector repels water, oil, and stains. It is more tailored than the Warrior shirt and definitely cooler to wear. It might run a little larger than stated size but the tailoring keeps ir from looking too large.

This shirt fastens with snaps instead of buttons although buttons are used for the collar and sleeves. Even though this comes as a long sleeved shirt you can turn it into a three-quarter sleeve shirt by folding the fabric up and buttoning it. Nice touch that! If you're in the hot sun it would be cooler with the sleeves buttoned up yet when night falls and the bugs come out you can simply revert to long sleeves. There are two large main (Velcro fastened) pockets on the top front of this shirt. Each of these two pockets has a zippered side document pocket behind it. There is a vent in the back to help keep you cool but in a pinch you could also roll up your boonie hat and carry it there.

I admit to not knowing what a "break away snap placket" is, and I plead ignorance in not understanding why there are two upside down mesh pockets (inside the front of the shirt) which could be used to great advantage if they had fasteners or were mounted in reverse. They might be used to provide extra stability by covering a holstered gun but perhaps I just don't understand the intention of the design. I'm sure that someone out there will enlighten me.
text_fidelity_b: BLACKHAWK Men's Tac Convertible Long Sleeve Shirt

text_fidelity_a:
MOON LENCE Camping Chairs, Compact Backpacking Chair Small Folding Chair Lawn Chair with Side Pockets Portable Lightweight for Hiking & Beach & Fishing To begin with, I am 5’7” and 265lbs woman with majority of the weight distributed within my middle part, so most of the backpacking chairs are passing by without even looking my way. I wave “hi-by” to them all the time when I see them without any regret.
This one is great! It loved me from the moment we met :). Comfortable, durable, nice looking and omg!!! lightweight and compact when folded!!!
I don’t understand those, who complain that it’s hard to assemble or to pack it back together. C’mon y’all! Read my little guide, and I hope it will help you somewhat.
Take it out of the packing bag, just slightly wave it in your hand and everything jumps together making the frame almost ready to go! All the parts are connected with rubbery string inside the aluminum poles, so it makes it magically come together.
Than check each elbow to make sure that it sits well together, pressing slightly towards the corners.
Take fabric, unfold it with letters on the top, so you can read it. Put on one bottom corner first. Than pulling by the loop put on a second bottom corner. Than put one of the top corners next (right one for right-handed person and left one for left-handed person). The last corner will be a little harder to put on. To make it much quicker and easier, set the frame on the ground facing towards you. Put one foot on the horizontal lower part of the frame under the fabric to insure that frame will stay in place and won’t move when you don’t need it to move. While holding the frame firmly with your foot, pull the last loop upwards with your right hand while pulling the aluminum pole towards you and slightly pressing it down. You’ll see that this way it gets very easy and takes about 5-10 seconds to put the last corner on. I showed this to my 6th grader and he picked up the order of assembling quickly.
The process of packing it back it also very easy, once you pay attention to those little white drawings on the aluminum base. You take apart the poles and fold them. First do one upper side pole and hold it with your hand. While holding it, twist the base, so sides of it will come together. Now you’ll have all four sides of the base and one upper pole together in your hand. Hold it tightly and, using an other hand, keep pulling apart and folding an other pole adding it to your hand for holding. To fix shorter legs in place just pull them slightly towards the middle and press them
down with the longer ones. When everything put together, just wrap that velcro cord around and voila!!! This took me about a minute the most. My son did it himself without my help too. It took him about 5-7 minutes when he was doing it for the first time.
Put everything on one side of triple-folded fabric and roll. It will be tight enough and will easily fit inside that carrying bag leaving some space for the small universal anti-sinking sand mat (14.5”x14.5”) that you can get for about $14-15. Buy it!!! It will make whole lot of difference! Your chair will never sink into sand or any other soft surface! Believe me you won’t regret. It will add just about 2-4oz of extra weight, but it worth it. Should of being included with each chair already, but it’s the problem of every chair of this category.
Once again, I love this chair as well as my whole family. I went and ordered more of them.
text_fidelity_b: MOON LENCE Camping Chairs, Compact Backpacking Chair Small Folding Chair Lawn Chair with Side Pockets Portable Lightweight for Hiking & Beach & Fishing

text_fidelity_a:
Snowshoes for Adult Unisex,Fully Adjustable Bindings, Lightweight Material, Hard Pack Grip Teeth,Outdoor Aluminum Alloy Material Really like these snowshoes. They are easy to adjust and stay on very well. The bag the shoes came in is first rate as are the poles. My only complaint is that the front binding only ratchets to a point then seem to hang up (it could be the strap end catching on the decking, or perhaps the hard boot material failing to flex)not a huge deal because it is snug enough. Also the pole carrying bag is separate from the shoe bag which means I got to remember to grab both. All in all a nice inexpensive snowshoe. Great for beginners or someone just needing a cheaper option.
12/29/11 UPDATE_ Got to try these out for the first time (not real deep snow- but enough to give them a trial run) These shoes are really nice. I tromped around for about 30 mins and had very few problems (main problem was some ice build up on my heel as I crossed a wet area and the water froze on my boot heel- not a big deal as it can happen with any snowshoe). The bindings did hold well and did not loosen at all. One shoe did seem to be toeing in a bit but that was probably an adjustment issue (it was also a new pair of boots I was trying out.) I'm gonna hopefully get out in some deeper snow next week (yea Lake Effect!)
1/15/12 UPDATE2- Finally got some REAL snow (18+ inches!) and tried these out at my hilly property in the deep woods. AMAZING how well they worked. It was pretty cold (hovering around 16° F in the sun) and the woods were untouched by anything but a few deer and turkeys. These shoes performed great. They never slipped and I did not have to adjust the bindings at all. They do seem to make a bit of noise as far as the bindings creaking (at these temps not to surprising), but nothing broke or loosened. Walked for a little over an hour; over logs, thru brush, uphill, downhill, level, tight twisty area, open fields, deep drifts, and even a snowmobile trail (that crosses the front of our property). These preformed as good as any other shoe. A bonus is I found I really liked the poles- so much so that I gave one to my wife and she really liked using it too. All in all a great purchase- These honestly hover on a 5 star rating- I did have to take away for the pole bag not being attached some way- also the poles are nearly impossible to closeup once they get cold (I think a bit of frost gets into the loosening cam and freezes the pole in place as once they warmed up there were no problems) also there is no place to store the rubber protection cap from the pole. The one show still seemed to toe in a bit- but I only notice it in very shallow snow (less than 6 inches) and the toe binding still only rachets to a certain point and then slips (still not an issue as it is snug enough). Oh and of course the noise factor (not real bad but your not gonna sneak up on anything with these on)

text_fidelity_a:
KUBEY KU085 Tactical Folding Knife G10 Handle Stainless Steel Blade Bearing Flipper Hunting Pocket Camping Survival Outdoor Knife (#KU087) Nice knife, especially at this price point. BUT, there are some issues. To me it appeared that this this knife is inferred as being spring assisted. It is most definitely not spring assisted as all other knives are determined to be. The thumb hole is difficult for me to use in one smooth motion. I thought that surely the flipper would be spring assisted, but no. It takes it to half open and no more. You need to use a wrist flip or two hands to finish the opening. That would not be much of a problem, but that makes it illegal to carry here in central Ohio. Sad.

One last thing. This blade is nowhere near 4 inches. It is measured at 3.5 inches. How does Kubey justify these irregularities? Perhaps this is just something being lost in translation.

This knife is super sharp. Locks up like a vault. No wobbles anywhere. It handles well. And it is beautiful. It is definitely worth the money as long as you know up front what you are buying. The build quality is there. The cosmetics are there. It doesn't need this type of advertising to sell. Thus the four stars. I would buy again and I will probably buy from Kubey again.

UPDATE 78/1/17:

The screws holding the clip have become loose. I am in the process of buying a torx bit set so I can tighten them. I wish that this clip could be switched for tip up carry, but the clip orientation cannot be changed.

I have recently discovered that this knife's mode of opening does not make it illegal to carry in Ohio since it requires manually beginning the opening sequence by putting pressure on the blade. Ohio laws are very ambiguous as to what is or is not legal to carry. Happy camper here.
text_fidelity_b: KUBEY KU085 Tactical Folding Knife G10 Handle Stainless Steel Blade Bearing Flipper Hunting Pocket Camping Survival Outdoor Knife (#KU087)

Meditation bench, Seiza Bench,It's Adjustable, Portable,Lightweight and Durable I'm over 60, and wanted to learn to sit seiza again; however sharp pains in my calfs and ankles made it difficult to maintain. I figured I could work up to it with this little bench, and it's doing the trick!! I gradually lowered the height to the lowest level...then I took a 7/8" diameter dowel and some scrap wood, and made a substitute "T" to fit under the seat. As my comfort with a height increases, I take the dowel and saw off about 1/4" at a time to reduce the height a bit. I'm finally able to sit seiza, even without the bench, without serious pain; I'll continue to lower the height and practice daily until I don't need the bench at all, but in the meantime, it makes sitting seiza for extended periods much more comfortable.

As others have noted, the bench has little padding (just a thin layer of dense foam), so this may not be comfortable if you're carrying much excess weight, since that would increase the pressure on your thighs. Since it looks like free returns aren't offered, you might consider buying a used bench (if available) to try it out less expensively; it's very sturdy, so a used one should work fine.

text_fidelity_a:
Klymit Maxfield Backpacking Tent, Lightweight 2-Person Tent for Camping and Hiking Honestly this tent is great, especially at the sale price it periodically goes down to. It is literally lighter than my previous 1-person tent. The stakes it comes with are great which is rare, plenty of guy-lines already attached and coiled up at the tie-off points, no issues with ventilation or heat retention in the 3-seasons it is designed for. The rainfly, footprint, and base of the tent all clip together quite nicely and have adjustment sliders to keep them correctly tensioned. The single piece pole assembly is a little counter-intuitive, but it works great once you orient it.

HOWEVER: get the footprint for it.

I bring a scrap of tarp to throw under the footprints of all my tents anyways, because a sharp, half buried rock can always ruin things, but you don't need to. A significant amount of the versatility and convenience goes away without the footprint that is designed for it, like the ability to throw the footprint and rainfly together as an emergency shelter in a few moments, or use it in an ultralight configuration to save even more weight.
The only potential concern i have is that with how light this material is, I don't know what long term durability will be. It is VERY light material, and that usually trades out durability. Time will tell.

text_fidelity_a:
Razor E300 Electric Scooter - 9" Air-filled Tires, Up to 15 mph and 10 Miles Range, White/Blue I just put some rubber bands on the throttle so it felt grippier. This thing is the most fun! I am 5'10 and weigh 180. It does have a hard time on hills but on flat land and down hill it can feel pretty fast. If you want to ride around town just choose flattest routes.

Like with a skateboard....once you learn the correct foot positions to ride comfortably, it is easy. I learned I put my feet on very similar as to my skateboards.

Since the throttle is either on or off with no inbetween....it can feel kind of jerky the first few times you ride it until you get used to that. You will learn it fast though....how to let off or turn on. Turning is not very tight radius so practice that if you arent used to riding one.
Prices are wild on these. I got mine last month for 260...the white e300 with the blue front forks. I see they are over 400 now. I think under 275 is a solid price if you want to play or plan to ride it to your local store or other near by places. Scooter laws vary state to state and where I am this is considered a toy and can be ridden on the sidewalks. Which....no one ever uses here anyway. We dont have bike lanes where I live either so I dont know if it would be legal to ride a bike lane in my state.

It is beefy and heavy and feels like a true machine rather than a toy. Mine charges fine, tires hold pressure fine, no issues at all.
I keep it inside because it flat states on the directions of use that extreme temps can effect the battery or even ruin it.
I have used it on street pavement, sidewalks, and fine gravel. I have never run out of charge on a trip but you CAN still kick scoot this old style if you do run out of charge.

I think it is fun, gets me out in the fresh air, saves some gas money.
text_fidelity_b: Razor E300 Electric Scooter - 9" Air-filled Tires, Up to 15 mph and 10 Miles Range, White/Blue

text_fidelity_a:
MinnKota Riptide 55 ST Bowmount Trolling Motor with i-Pilot and No Foot Pedal (55lbs Thrust, 54" Shaft) I bought one of these for my 18' Carolina Skiff. I also bought the quick release mount. I bought the quick release mount so I could remove the trolling motor when travelling long distances with the boat. I fish from MD to the Gulf and bouncing down the road wouldn't be be good for it. First impression is that I'm going to like it a lot. I've been in the water twice using the trolling motor, both times in salt water, which is where I spend most of my fishing time. Installation was easy and deploying and retracting the ST55 is also easy. The iPilot anchor function worked well in 1.5 mph currents and 12 knot winds. I'll try it in the 8kt currents in the OBX in August. I like the iPilot control unit and no foot pedal because I'm not restricted to a certain place in the boat. I maxed it out and was surprised at how strong the motor was. I used the motor for about 2 hours and battery drain was about 1.4 volts from 14.2 to 12.8. Totally acceptable, especially for the size boat and winds. The instructions call for a 60 amp inline circuit breaker, however, I'm using a 40 amp and it was fine on full power. I've given it a 4 star rating right now and will return to add more to this review once I've used the programming features of the iPilot.

Update 24 Feb 15: I have nothing but praise for Min-Kota and the RipTide ST55. I've put about 70 hours on this motor and spent many hours in the anchor mode against 2-3 knot tides. I didn't use my boat anchor once during the summer and fall months because the RipTide's anchor function is spot on. I mainly fish in saltwater and I've used it from Florida, to North Carolina, to Maryland and its performance is outstanding. The only down side is it doesn't have automatic deploy and retrieve. I know Min-Kota is working on one. I love the iPilot! I can use it from anywhere on the boat and only have to remember when facing backwards, left is right and right is left. Duh. Most definitely 5 STARS
text_fidelity_b: MinnKota Riptide 55 ST Bowmount Trolling Motor with i-Pilot and No Foot Pedal (55lbs Thrust, 54" Shaft)

text_fidelity_a:
Trek Tents 10 x 14' Canvas Cabin Tent Khaki Yes, it Does work. Tension is the key.
Looking at the pictures of this tent you can see that it Should work, but you Doubt it, right??
Here on the NorthCoast of California right next to that big body of water, we have normal breezes running around 15 mph. When it gets a bit Windy it'll run around 35 mph. Then there's when it gets brisk ;>
It's still hanging out in the place I'd staked it when other tents had hopped the fence and wandered down the street.
I'd gotten tired of having to replace those nylon things every year or two and wanted something a lot more permanent in a temporary structure.
The canvas is IT for me!
I like that they'd used a white for the roofing giving you a more open feeling than you'd have otherwise if they'd gone with the base color.
I'm very happy with the construction. Tabs, zipper-pulls, netting in doors and windows. The floor is sturdy enough to dance on.
The tie-downs and stakes need to be replaced. I'm really very disappointed that this tent has such a poor finish after all the fine work they'd done for the main structure.
The skinny and very stretchy nylon strings and skinny smooth metal pins they give you stretch when dampened and the pegs pull out. It's an easy fix, not to worry. Just get a length of REAL Rope and re-do the tie-downs and buy a handful of those lovely orange plastic pegs that have teeths and you'll Keep the proper tension in the roof you need for when you get 3 inches of rain dumped on you, even With the rain-fly covering the roof. You will of course need to re-adjust the tie-downs after this happens. Good News!! Even with a couple of tub fulls of rain on the tent that you'll need to dump off, the tent Remains STANDING!

UPDATE:
After the ground got SUPER saturated with days of rain and some SERIOUS winds and GUSTS, it's collapsed Twice and the rain fly has completely died. The tie down banding along one edge RIPPED OFF and the ties From the tent to the Center pole ripped off.
The rain fly needs to be anchored SEPARATELY if you also have issue with winds. Since it's integrated with the tent, it causes Severe wall flapping and even with heavy duty metal tent pegs doing their Best, it still collapses.
NOT A HAPPY CAMPER :(((
2ND UPDATE:
We have some fairly Serious WIND and RAIN issues here and this tent does NOT hold up. The first thing that went was the rain fly, as you might have noted from my First post.
I'd replaced the useless tie down strings that came with and got some screw in the ground pegs to hold the metal framing, also noted above.
Now, the loops are ripping out.
I'D RETURN THIS TENT IF I COULD. Not sure what I'm going to do with a $600 bit of canvas that I CANNOT USE AS A TENT :(((
(too bad the vendor doesn't monitor these reviews)
text_fidelity_b: Trek Tents 10 x 14' Canvas Cabin Tent Khaki

Stanley The Quadvac Trigger Action Mug, Canvas, 16OZ This is the best thermos I've owned to date, but it's far from perfect.

If you put piping hot coffee in it, it will keep it hot for about 45 minutes, and keep it warm for about 2 more hours after that. I haven't used it for cold drinks.

I love the handle style; that's my favorite part about it. Most handled thermoses have this infuriating issue of the mouthpiece never lining up properly with where the handle is, so you always have to hold them weirdly to drink from them. On this thermos, the handle is fabric, and can be adjusted 360 degrees around the thermos, so no matter where the mouthpiece ends up, you can just adjust the handle to be right where you need it. the other nice thing about the fabric handle is that you won't break it by bumping it into things or dropping it.

The worst part about this thing is cleaning it. The entire head of it is very complex, with lots of moving parts, springs, and plastic bits - ALL of which are submerged in whatever you are drinking. So, when you take the lid off, you have disassemble the whole thing and either soak all the parts, or wash them all individually. Don't be lazy and put off cleaning it until the next day or you'll have whatever you drank caked all though the innards. If you don't mind keeping it clean, it's really nice. I'm very happy with it.

The so-so: I didn't like the square pack, packed to 14" H x 13" W x 4" D. Fit in an 11L compression sack (excluding stakes and poles), and compressed nicely in that regard. You can use this with lump charcoal or briquettes. All you need to do is light some newspaper in the bottom and let it sit for a couple minutes... before you know it you will see a vortex of flame and some red hot charcoal.

I use this when I grill as well as when I visit state and national parks. There's nothing quite like being able to cook your lunch in the picnic area without all of the waiting for your coals to get hot.

Pros:
- Lights all coal quickly and evenly.
- Lightweight
- Cools quickly
- Feels solid and the handle stays cool

Cons:
- The second handle really isn't necessary. It can get in the way... luckily it's easy to remove.
- Doesn't hold enough coal to completely fill the kettle... maybe I use too much when I sear steaks but if you ask me... 2 of these is a better deal.

Overall this is one of those "must haves" for anyone who uses charcoal to grill.
text_fidelity_b: Rapidfire Chimney Starter

I have the 1200 yard spool. For the cost difference go with more and fill up your many reels many more times!

text_fidelity_a: gearoot Remote Control Electric Heated Socks with Rechargeable Li-ion Batteries Winter Warm Cotton Socks for Hiking Skiing Cycling Fishing The picture shows that the heat is along the sides.  I had hoped that with heating elements along the sides would keep my entire foot warm.  Nope.  The heating elements are concentrated on the upper section of the foot, over the toes and not all the way to my ankle .  Now for the batteries - OMG these batteries are THICK!  Nearly 3/4ths of an inch thick!  I charged them up and thought, oh well, if I didn't want to wear my boots...because I wouldn't be able to zip or tie either of my pairs of winter boots over the tops of the socks because of the thick batteries.  Now the reason in particular that I gravitated to this pair of socks was the remote control.  That works fine.  I mean, if I want to change the heat level or turn them off, bending down and pushing a button on both socks to change heat or turn them off seemed stupid to me.  So I can say the remote works well.  As for the heat, I'm just not happy with the concentration just on the top-front of each foot.  The picture is misleading - state that the heating elements are ONLY on the top-front of each sock so consumers are better informed.  Last, does the battery packs HAVE to be that thick?  You literally cannot have these on and put a leg up under you or the battery pack will jab your leg (or any way you are not simply sitting with each foot straight in front of you).  I gave them four stars because they do work, just not in the way I expected they should.

text_fidelity_a:
WOLF GRIZZLY Titanium Cutlery, Lightweight Fork and Spoon, Cutlery Set with Case for Camping Backpacking and Travel When traveling I like to carry a spoon capable of scooping Ben & Jerry’s ice cream since hotels usually only have disposable plastic spoons. This spoon fails the ice cream scoop test, although it puts up a fight before it bends. Since if fails that test it does not meet my needs. I did not get this for camping, which is the main use for this product. When I go camping I use plastic dinnerware which has worked fine for me.

Why does this “cutlery” set lack a knife? That is a significant omission for a "cutlery" set. $30 is too much to pay for a thin fork and spoon. These are lighter weight than flatware you would use at home, but they are about the same weight as all the other utensils designed for travel or camping. Titanium costs more because it is a rare metal, not because it is superior. If you are traveling by plane and security decides to confiscate your fork, you will be out $15.

For a $30 set that advertises that it is strong, I would expect to get a spoon that is capable of scooping premium ice cream without bending. I just reviewed a stainless-steel spoon that was of higher quality, was much stronger, and cost $3. I mainly use these for typical vacation and work travel, not multi-day hiking and camping, so weight does not matter much. If you are camping then this set is fine, but so is plastic.
text_fidelity_b: WOLF GRIZZLY Titanium Cutlery, Lightweight Fork and Spoon, Cutlery Set with Case for Camping Backpacking and Travel
